title: Why You Must Say No To Pleading Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns against giving in to student pleading for reduced academic demands, arguing that even a single concession opens the door to constant negotiation over every future assignment and lesson. He walks through the concrete downstream costs: students come to expect novelty or relief as the norm, treat ordinary assignments as disappointments, and absorb the message that the activity being begged away from has no inherent value, which undermines the broader goal of instilling a love of hard, worthwhile work. His prescribed response is to say no immediately, without pausing to consider the request, since any hesitation signals that the decision is negotiable. The piece frames consistent refusal not as rigidity for its own sake but as the only way to teach students that struggle and rigor, not relief from them, are where real satisfaction is found.
points: Giving in to student pleading even once opens the floodgates, turning every future planned activity into an expected negotiation.
Conceding to a request signals that the activity being begged away from lacks inherent value, undermining the broader goal of building a love of hard work.
The recommended response to pleading is to say no immediately without pausing, since any hesitation signals the decision might be negotiable.
Consistent refusal to negotiate assignments is framed as necessary for building genuine student maturity, ownership, and appreciation for challenge.
quotes: Once you give in, even one time, you’ll open the floodgates and every planned activity will feel like a negotiation.
Anything less than novelty or surprise relief will be a crushing blow. This isn’t an exaggeration. No matter the age, give an inch and they’ll want a mile.
If you give in to please your students, you’ll send the message that the activity in question is inherently distasteful. It doesn’t have value or reward in and of itself.
The best way to respond to pleading is to immediately say no. Because once you pause, you’re in trouble.
Show your students that in the midst of struggle is where they’ll find beauty and the greatest joy.
